[00:00] Visitor: Okay, it's recording. We're sitting in the workshop, it's early, the light is coming in sideways through the door. Can you tell me how you started with this work? Mender: I started by accident, really. My uncle had a shop that sold old bowls, mostly things people brought in from houses that were being cleared. Half of them were cracked. He used to throw the cracked ones in a box under the counter, and I was the boy who sat next to that box all day. I would take them out and hold the pieces together with my hands, just to see what the bowl had looked like before. I was maybe eleven. Nobody taught me anything at first. I only wanted to know where each crack started and where it was going. That question never left me, if I'm honest. It is still the first thing I look for when a bowl comes in.

[00:58] Visitor: Where was the shop? Mender: In the old part of town, near the river, on a lane so narrow two carts could not pass. It is gone now. There is a bank there. My uncle closed it in 1987, the year my aunt died, and he gave me the box of broken bowls as if it was an inheritance. In a way it was. Forty one bowls. I counted them that night on the floor of my room. Some of them I still have. That one on the shelf with the brown rim, the third from the left, that came from the box. It took me nine years to find a way to mend it that I was not ashamed of. Nine years for one bowl. People laugh when I say that, but I mean it as the most ordinary thing in the world.

[02:01] Visitor: What did you learn first, technically? Mender: Patience is the boring answer, so let me give you the real one. The first thing I learned is that glue is a lie. When you glue a bowl you are pretending nothing happened. The bowl looks whole from across the room, and then you pick it up and you feel it is dead. It does not ring. You tap it with your finger and there is nothing there. So I stopped gluing. I started looking at how people in other places mended things. The staples, the old way, where you drill tiny holes on both sides of a crack and bridge it with a little metal staple, like stitches. The lacquer way, with gold on top. And the plain way, just a line of resin that does not hide. Each one says something different about what happened to the bowl.

[03:12] Visitor: You mentioned the gold. People here call that kinsugi, right? Mender: People call it many things. The Japanese word is the one everybody knows. In Chinese there is a word that means gold repair, and the old craftsmen I learned from in Jingdezhen did not make a big philosophy about it. I went there in March, when I was twenty six, and stayed almost two years. I lived above a kiln that fired celadon, the green one, they called it cellar don when they spoke English to tourists, which made me laugh every time. They did not care about the poetry of the gold. They cared whether the line was clean and whether the bowl could hold hot water again. That was the test. Can you pour into it. Can you drink from it. If not, you have made an ornament, not a bowl.

[04:20] Mender: I want to say something about that, actually, because people ask me about the philosophy all the time now. I think every crack is a record of the hands that used it. That is the only philosophy I have. A bowl cracks because somebody used it, every day, for years. It went into hot water and cold water. It was knocked against a tap. It was dropped by a child, maybe. When I mend the crack I am not fixing a mistake. I am writing down that somebody lived with this bowl. The gold or the staple or the resin is just the ink. Some people want the line to disappear. I understand why. But for me, if the line disappears, so does the person who used it. I would rather keep them.

[05:31] Visitor: Do you remember the first bowl you were proud of? Mender: Yes. A small tea bowl, dark, with a crack that ran from the rim almost to the foot, like a river on a map. It belonged to an old woman who lived two doors down. She brought it wrapped in a towel and said, this was my husband's, he drank from it every morning for thirty years, can you make it so I can drink from it. I worked on it for three weeks. When I gave it back she poured tea into it right there, in the shop, standing up, and drank. She did not say anything. She just nodded. That nod is still the best thing anybody has ever said about my work. I think about her more than I think about any famous collector who came later.

[06:40] Visitor: What happens to you when you work? Mender: When I sit with one bowl for a whole day, my own day gets quieter. It is hard to explain to people who live by the clock. In the morning I have a hundred thoughts. Money, my knee, my daughter's exams, the roof. Then I take the bowl in my hands and I start to look at the crack, and after an hour or so the thoughts get further away. They do not go. They just get further away, like voices in another room. By the afternoon there is only the line and my breathing. I do not call it meditation. I call it work. But my wife says I come home a different man on the days I mend, and she is usually right about me.

[07:44] Visitor: Do you drink tea while you work? Mender: All day. Not fancy. Whatever is in the tin. Lately a don cong from a friend who goes to the mountains every spring, very fragrant, almost like fruit. Sometimes a rock tea, the roasted kind. I use a small clay pot from ee shing that my teacher gave me when I left. It is not valuable. It has a chip on the spout that I have never mended, on purpose. People ask me, you of all people, why do you not mend your own pot? And I say, because it reminds me that not everything needs me. The pot works. The chip does not stop the tea. Some things you leave alone. That is also part of the craft, knowing when to keep your hands off.

[08:50] Mender: There is something I tell students about the kettle. You hear the water before it boils. First small bubbles, like fish eyes, then a sound like wind in pine trees, then the rolling boil. The old books describe it this way. If you are rushing, you miss the stages, you just wait for the click of the electric kettle. But if you listen, the water is telling you something all the time. A crack is the same. It tells you where it is going to run before it runs. You listen to the bowl when you tap it. A healthy bowl sings. A bowl with a hidden crack sounds flat, like it has a cold. Twelve years it took me before I could hear the difference every time.

[09:56] Visitor: Twelve years? Mender: Twelve, maybe thirteen. I am not good with numbers. Ask my wife, she does the accounts. The point is, it is slow. Everything in this work is slow, and the world is not slow, so there is always a fight. Clients want the bowl back next week. Galleries want twenty pieces for an exhibition. Somebody on the internet wants me to make a video in thirty seconds. I understand. I also need to eat. But the bowl does not care about any of that. The resin cures when it cures. If you hurry it, it fails in a year, and then the bowl is worse than before, because now it has two wounds. So I have learned to say no. Not often. But enough.

[11:02] Visitor: How do you choose which way to mend a bowl? Mender: I ask the bowl, and I ask the person. The bowl tells me what it can take. A thin porcelain cup cannot take staples, it would shatter when you drill. A heavy country bowl can take staples very well, and it looks honest with them, like an old farmer with patched trousers. Then I ask the person what the bowl means to them. If it was their grandmother's, sometimes they want the gold, because it feels like an honour. If they use it every day and do not want to think about it, maybe a plain line. I try not to impose my taste. It is their bowl. I am only the one who holds it for a while in between.

[12:10] Mender: A mended bowl is like a person who kept going. Mending it, I mend something in me. I did not always know that. When I was young I thought I was fixing objects. Then my father got sick, and for two years I mended bowls at night after the hospital, because it was the only thing I could do with my hands that worked. Everything else was out of my control. The doctors, the money, his pain. But the bowl, I could put the bowl back together, one piece at a time. I think that is when I understood that the work was not only for the bowl. It was keeping me together too. I do not say this to clients. I am saying it to you because you asked properly.

[13:18] Visitor: Thank you. Can I ask about the staples, the old method? Mender: Of course. It is my favourite, to be honest, even though the gold is what people pay for. You mark the crack, then you drill tiny holes, not all the way through, at an angle, on both sides of the line. Then you make the staple from copper or brass, bend it, and set it into the holes while the metal is a little warm, so it pulls the two sides together as it cools. The old menders walked from village to village with their drills and a little stool, shouting in the street. My teacher in Jingdezhen still did it like that when he was a young man, he said, in the nineteen fifties. A good stapled bowl can last another hundred years. Longer than the person who used it. Longer than me.

[14:25] Visitor: Are there many people still doing it? Mender: Very few. I know of maybe six in this country who do it well. There are many more who do the gold, because it is popular and because you can learn the basics from a video. That is fine. I am not a snob. But the staple work needs strong hands and a lot of failure. You break many bowls learning. I broke more bowls than I mended in my first five years. My uncle would have been furious. Every broken bowl was a little funeral. I kept the pieces of those too, in a second box. Sometimes I use the shards to test resin colours. Nothing is wasted. Not even the mistakes.

[15:30] Visitor: You said you want to teach. Mender: I want to teach this, so the craft does not stop with me. That is the real worry now, not money, not my knee. If I die tomorrow, the box of bowls goes to my daughter, and she loves me, but she is studying to be an engineer. She has no interest. That is her right. So I have started taking two students on Saturdays. A young man who works in a bakery during the week, and a woman who used to be a nurse. They are good. The nurse especially, her hands are steady and she is not afraid of blood, she jokes, though there is no blood, only resin. They are not ready yet. Maybe in three years. Maybe five.

[16:41] Visitor: What do you teach them first? Mender: Not the drill. Not the gold. I teach them to sit with a bowl and say nothing for an hour. They hate it. The baker especially, he wants to do something. But you have to learn to look before you touch. Where does the crack begin? Is it one crack or two that met? Did it start from a knock on the rim or from heat at the foot? A bowl tells its whole history if you are quiet enough. Then, only then, we talk about what to do. My uncle never taught me anything, but he let me sit next to the box for years. Maybe that was the teaching. I did not know it at the time. The nurse understood it in a week. The baker took two months, but now he is the one who reminds me to slow down when I reach for the drill too early, which is funny, and also exactly right.

[17:50] Visitor: Is there a bowl you could not mend? Mender: Many. But one I remember. A white bowl, very thin, from a collector who had dropped it in his kitchen. Fourteen pieces. He wanted it perfect, invisible, so he could sell it later at the old price. I told him I could make it whole, I could make it hold tea again, but I could not make it invisible, and I would not lie to the next owner. He took it to someone else. I heard later it was sold at auction as undamaged. That made me sad for a week. Not because of the money. Because the record was erased. Somebody's life with that bowl was erased so that another person could pay more for a lie.

[18:58] Mender: You know, my wife says I talk to the bowls. I do, a little. Not out loud so much. More like, okay, where are you going, show me. Last winter there was a big bowl from the coast, a fish bowl, very heavy, with salt in the cracks from years by the sea. I soaked it for nine days to get the salt out. Every morning I changed the water and tasted it, a tiny bit, on my finger. Day one, very salty. Day nine, nothing. Only then could I start. You cannot mend over salt. It comes back through the resin, like a memory you did not deal with. I think that is true for people too, but I am not a philosopher, I only know bowls.

[20:05] Visitor: Do the bowls ever surprise you? Mender: All the time. A bowl will look simple, a plain brown thing from a farmhouse, and then when I clean it there is a maker's mark under the foot that nobody saw for a hundred years. Or there is an old repair under the dirt, a staple somebody set before I was born, very neat, better than my work. That is humbling. You think you are the first person to care about this bowl and then you find the fingerprint of someone who cared before you, with worse tools and more skill. I always leave the old repairs. I mend around them. It feels like a conversation with a man I will never meet. He did his part, I do mine, and maybe someone after me does theirs.

[21:12] Visitor: Has the work changed how you see your own life? Mender: Yes, but slowly, the way water changes a stone. When I was thirty I was angry about a lot of things. My uncle's shop closing, my father, money, the people who bought my bowls and never used them. Now I am sixty one, and the anger is still there sometimes, but it has a line of gold through it, if you understand me. I have been broken a few times. My knee, my marriage nearly, my father's death. Each time something held. Not perfectly. You can see the line. But I can still hold hot water, so to speak. I can still be used. I think that is all I want from my own life, the same as from a bowl.

[22:20] Mender: One more thing about the students, because I do not want to sound like I am only worried. The other Saturday the baker mended his first cup by himself. A small thing, a cheap cup from the market, one clean crack. He used the plain resin, no gold, and the line was a little crooked. When he finished he poured water into it and held it up to the window to see if it leaked. It did not leak. He laughed like a child. I had not heard him laugh before, he is a serious young man. I thought, there, that is it, that is the whole thing passed on, in one laugh. The rest is only practice. Twenty years of practice, but only practice.

[23:28] Visitor: Last question. What would you want someone to feel when they drink from a bowl you mended? Mender: That they are not the first. That somebody held this before them, and something happened, and it was not the end. I would like them to feel a little less alone, maybe. And then I would like them to forget about me completely and just drink their tea. The best mend is the one you notice once, and then it becomes part of the bowl, part of your mornings. Like a scar on your hand you stopped seeing years ago. If they think about me every time, I have made it too loud. A bowl should be used. That is all it ever wanted.

[24:21] Visitor: Thank you. I'll stop the recording here.
